groups.content:
The barricade myth and the cost of the project

In chapter eight, Hart examines a [36] that the boulevards were designed to stop revolutionaries from blocking the streets. He accepts that military concerns influenced some routes, but shows that they were seldom the [37] for building a street. Hart also explains how the work was financed. Loans were to be repaid through [38] along the new streets. However, as costs rose, Haussmann came to depend on [39] which Parliament did not know about. This eventually led to his [40] from office in 1870.

questions.explanation: Answer: penguin Paragraph 1: 'the name ' penguin ' was originally used for the great auk'.
Answer: rock Paragraph 3: the egg 'was laid directly onto the bare rock , without any nest'.
Answer: pattern Paragraph 3: 'it is believed that each one had a unique pattern '.
Answer: bait Paragraph 5: 'sailors killed them in their thousands for food and for bait '.
Answer: feathers Paragraph 5: 'the auks were hunted for their soft feathers , which were used to stuff mattresses and pillows'.
Answer: TRUE Earlier hunting had little effect, but ' This changed from the sixteenth century onwards ', when sailors killed the birds in their thousands.
Answer: FALSE ' the ban was difficult to enforce in such remote places '.
Answer: FALSE As the birds became rarer, ' Museums and wealthy private collectors began to compete for skins and eggs ', and prices rose.
Answer: FALSE They believed it was a witch that had caused a storm, and ' they killed it '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The island was destroyed and the surviving birds moved, but the passage does not say how many birds died.
Answer: NOT GIVEN They worked for a dealer, but nothing is said about how much they were paid.
Answer: TRUE ' there were unconfirmed reports of sightings off Newfoundland in 1852 '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The surviving skins and eggs are described, but there is no mention of any plan to bring the species back.
Answer: F Section F: agroforestry farms ' can provide habitats for hundreds of species ', store carbon and protect the soil.
Answer: G Section G describes the Cocoa Stewardship Council, its members and its standards.
Answer: A Section A: cocoa ' is also found in drinks, biscuits, breakfast cereals and ice cream ', as well as skin creams and medicines.
Answer: H Section H: ' researchers are investigating whether a tiny insect could help farmers produce more cocoa ': the midge.
Answer: B Section B: ' In 1980, world production was around 1.6 million tonnes a year ; by the early 2020s... around five million tonnes'.
Answer: E Section E: two million poor families depend on cocoa; if demand fell, ' it would be these families who would suffer most '.
Answer: C Section C: ' Populations of western chimpanzees, pygmy hippopotamuses and many species of forest birds have fallen sharply. '

text.en: Its membership has increased rapidly in recent years.
It requires members to make inspection results public.
Its standards took a long time to agree.
It carries out inspections on farms every month.
It has been praised by all environmental groups.

questions.explanation: Answer: B, C ' Its standards were developed gradually, through years of negotiation ' (C), and ' Members must also publish the results of the independent inspections ' (B). Critics say inspections are too infrequent (D).
Answer: solid Section A: 'Cocoa butter stays solid at room temperature'.
Answer: forest elephant Section C: 'the fate of the forest elephant ... only a few hundred are thought to remain'.
Answer: farm boundaries Section G: 'growers must map their farm boundaries using satellite data'.
Answer: pollination Section H: 'If we can boost pollination , farmers could produce the same amount of cocoa on much less land'.

text.en: It presents a completely new theory about the history of Paris.
It is mainly intended for specialist historians.
It takes a different approach from earlier books on the subject.
It considers a wide range of aspects of the transformation of Paris.

questions.explanation: Answer: D ' Drawing on politics, engineering, public health and economics , as well as the letters and diaries of ordinary Parisians'. The book will interest a wide audience (B).

text.en: She explains why Hart is interested in the topic.
She suggests that Hart has ignored some evidence.
She compares Hart's view with that of other historians.
She praises Hart for his use of Haussmann's memoirs.

questions.explanation: Answer: B Haussmann's memoirs show he wanted the poor removed, and ' Hart does not really explain why these statements should be set aside '.

text.en: It contains several errors.
It repeats information from earlier chapters.
It will not appeal to most non-specialist readers.
It relies on out-of-date research.

questions.explanation: Answer: C Specialists will find it valuable, ' but I suspect that many general readers will skip it '.

text.en: It ignores the role of the army in eastern Paris.
It is based on too little evidence.
It repeats a widely accepted view.
It presents a persuasive case.

questions.explanation: Answer: D ' he argues convincingly that they were rarely the main reason '. He does mention eastern Paris (A), and he challenges the common view (C).

text.en: the quality of the illustrations
the author's admiration for Haussmann
the originality of the research
the author's conclusions about the future of Paris

questions.explanation: Answer: C ' What makes the book stand out is the quality of Hart's archival research. ' His use of property records is 'genuinely original'. The maps and photographs are weaknesses (A).
Answer: NO ' It is not a pleasant picture, but it is a compelling one ', and the walk is 'one of the most memorable passages'.
Answer: YES These chapters ' provide an essential foundation for what follows '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The review says they were forced out, but nothing about whether they returned.
Answer: NO ' the total cost of the project rose far beyond the original estimates '.
Answer: H (popular belief) ' the widely repeated claim that the boulevards were designed mainly to prevent revolutionaries from blocking the streets '.
Answer: D (main motive) Military considerations ' were rarely the main reason for building a particular street '.
Answer: I (increasing land values) Loans ' were to be repaid from the rising value of land along the new streets '.
Answer: B (hidden arrangements) Haussmann relied on ' complicated financial arrangements that were hidden from Parliament '.
Answer: F (forced removal) ' He was eventually dismissed in January 1870 ', before the project or the Empire ended.
